entry.title: Rania
entry.summary: Can you first introduce where you’re from, where you grew up, all…
entry.content:
Can you first introduce where you’re from, where you grew up, all of that?

Yeah, of course. I guess I have two sides of mine. I have my father's side, he's completely Moroccan. He moved to the Netherlands in his twenties, where he met my mum. On my mum's side, she was born in the Netherlands. She's Dutch, but all of her family, her parents and beyond, are also from Morocco. So I've got my mum who's Dutch, but ethnically Moroccan, and then my father's completely Moroccan. I was born in the Netherlands as well, and then I moved away at about ten or eleven years old to England, together with my parents and my brother – who was also born in the Netherlands – because my father found work. And yeah, ever since then – I'm twenty-three now – I've been in England really.

 

Do you have citizenship here?

No. [laughs] I moved here pre-Brexit. I'm still on a Dutch passport, and I've got settled status. No English passport yet. My brother has an English passport. He's the only one in our family who does.

 

Do you feel more connected to the Dutch side or the English side?

I think the English side. I mean, it makes sense. I've been here longer, but I've also spent most of my proper growth years here. I know people often talk about childhood as being the years where you're forming, and that's true. But I also think that adolescence and your teenage years are when you start making your decisions about what you like, what you think, and what your opinions on the world are. And those have been shaped in England. Being at university, learning how to think about the world, being in secondary and sixth form. Those have all been here. And because of that, I feel like a lot of my thought process has been shaped in quite an English way.

It is interesting though, because although I came here about ten or eleven, I still have a remnant of an accent. So because of that, I feel like there is always a part of me that won't be completely British. Not in a sense where I don't connect to the culture, but I think the first talking point with people is often ‘where are you from?’, even if I connect better with England. So there is always that little distance. That few percent that means that I'm distanced from the culture. Alongside, of course, the way I look. If you look at me, I'm not British, I'm ethnically Moroccan. So I don't think I'm 100% anything. If I had to choose, I would say England is most familiar.

 

So if you were introducing yourself, would you say you're English or Dutch?

See, that's so interesting because it happens a lot, right? Especially since I don't have a British accent. I've got some remnants of a weird Frankenstein accent. My go-to response is ‘what do you mean?’, ‘in what way?’, and people always look at me quite puzzled. I had to do that last week when meeting somebody. She's an international student from Egypt, and I was thinking ‘oh gosh, how do I approach this?’ Because, you know, we're neighbours, Morocco and Egypt, but then do I really connect with that? So I just hit her with a ‘what do you mean?’. They often say ‘tell me everything’. So I have to give them the whole story, because I feel like if I tell somebody I'm British in England, they're going to raise an eyebrow; ‘no, you're not’, which they're right about. Dutch is sometimes what I go for if the setting is right. For example, if I'm at a conference and lots of the people there are from Europe or from Germany, I often lean towards Dutch.

But I feel like most people who ask ‘where are you from?’ are really asking like, ‘why do you look the way you do?’. So I feel like I have to add in the fact that I'm ethnically Moroccan, even though that opens doors such as ‘do you speak Arabic?’ and then I have to let them down. I remember once in my first week at work there was this employee from Egypt who saw my name and was like ‘oh, where are you from?’ and I had to do the whole spiel. And then he asked ‘do you speak Arabic?’ And you can just see them let down when I have to tell them I don't. Or a taxi driver asking me why I look that way or why my name is Rania.

Long story short, to be safe, I tell people the whole story because I often feel like they will dig for something. If I say that I'm Moroccan, they will ask if I speak Arabic. And if I'm not able to say that I do, I'll have to explain that I lived in the Netherlands. If I say I'm Dutch, people will question why I look the way I do, why my name is Rania, and why I'm five-foot-two instead of a huge towering giant. And then if I say I'm English, while I'm in England, people often can tell I'm not. If I'm on a holiday abroad, I will often just stick with England or something like that.

 

So you're being asked that wherever you go.

Yeah, yeah. I do notice that I'm asked that a lot, which makes sense because I've got a little bit of an accent. I don't look white British or anything like that. So I don't think it's always people trying to separate me. I think a lot of people are just curious. They see someone who looks different or has a different name. A lot of these people, like they might be from Egypt, are very curious. Maybe they think you're from where they're from, or maybe they know somebody from a culture they think you're from. I think it's inevitable, even though it's sometimes a hard question to answer.

 

And in the Netherlands, can people tell that you haven't spent as much time there? Do you have any sort of an accent when you speak Dutch, for example? Because I imagine the Netherlands now is a pretty multicultural country, so I'm a little surprised that you would be asked so often ‘where are you from?’ while you’re there if you're speaking Dutch at a native level.

Yeah, you're totally right. The Netherlands is hugely multicultural. A lot of my family is from Amsterdam specifically. Hugely multicultural. Whether my Dutch has slipped a little bit? Yes, especially in my written Dutch. But obviously people don't notice that when you're spending time abroad. I have noticed- I was so sad. I got a phone call from my aunt the other year and she was talking to me. I often hear ‘oh, wow, your Dutch is really good still’. But she said something like ‘oh, it sounds like you've got an English accent when speaking Dutch’, and I was thinking ‘oh, no!’ [laughs] ‘Oh, gosh. An accent on speaking English AND on speaking Dutch?’ So there’s definitely that indicator. And of course, I don't have a Dutch face either. People are curious to know if not whether I'm from there, whether my parents are from there either. I think that's to be expected, to be honest.

 

And does that bother you then, the fact that you're always having to answer this and always giving caveats?

Yes and no. 99.999% percent of the time people who ask this aren't trying to be discriminatory. They're saying this out of genuine curiosity, and they seem super excited when they ask that. So I can never be mad at that. But it is difficult because I'm having to explain these cultures and it feels like there’s a tag against my name. And although I love all of the places I am from, it feels like I can never distance myself from them, often this is the first thing people want to know about me.

And I guess I feel it's a bit of a shame as well that although I have these labels to my name, I don't have that strong of a resonance with my culture. So I have to tell people I am from Morocco because there's no way of distancing myself from the fact that I'm Moroccan. I've got a Moroccan name after all, but I can't speak the language, I haven't been there in so many years, and I feel like I'm mis-selling myself by adding that to my name. But I have to add it to my name because it is part of me. It's a weird internal mixed bag of feelings.

 

Do you wish you had more of a connection to Morocco then, for example?

Yeah, it is really difficult having the name, having the face, having the family lineage and not even being able to speak the language. I'd be lying if I said I don't feel a sense of shame when I have to tell people that I'm not as connected as I should be.

For example, I think if you take minorities in the Netherlands, like the Moroccan minority, they often have quite a strong feeling towards their culture, a sense of pride, because they're a minority and it's the little piece of home that they have left that they brought into the country. I admire that to a certain degree. I often think we talk a lot about the bad parts of nationalism – there are many, many, many parts that are bad – but on the patriotic side, there's something so nice about having a place that's home or feels homely, to have something that you can connect with. A culture. Meeting somebody in public who’s completely different to you but you share and you know the same love for the same food, or you've been to the same places, or you understand that depth through language.

I think it's hard to replicate, and unfortunately, as much as I love to be more connected with my culture now, I fear that the way that I interact with it is always going to feel more like a tourist to my own culture. The way I have to go out of my way to learn the language, or visit these super touristy spots in Morocco that any native would never go to. It sometimes feels like I'm putting on a costume to my own culture. I sometimes envy people who can say ‘oh, yeah, me? I'm Moroccan. I know everything about Morocco. I grew up there. It's my home’. I remember when I told that Egyptian co-worker that I didn't speak the language, he said ‘oh, it's fine, you don't need to know it’ and I said ‘I feel like there's a little bit that you will never be able to connect with if you don't speak the language’. I think if you speak the language, you get so much closer than if you don't. I remember him agreeing with that, and I think it's true. There's always going to be that distance unless I cross it, which is going to take quite a while because it's not an easy language.

 

Are you trying to learn it?

At the moment, I'm not. No. I've been really focussed on all sorts of things. I mean, I'm making excuses here, to be honest with you. Part of me is focussing on trying to secure what is immediate. My immediate career in the UK, in England, my immediate degree here and everything to shape my new world here. It's even harder when Morocco feels so far away, when I don't have a close, tight-knit family that I'm connected with from Morocco. I don't have a lot of Moroccan friends or anything like that. It feels like this other world that’s just out of reach. It's something I have to try harder for if it's something I want, which I haven't yet. That and it being quite a challenging language has stopped me so far as to learning it. But I really hope to be able to make it more of a priority at some point.

 

From the sounds of it though you have been there before.

I have been there when I was super young. We used to go every few years, and then the last time was eight years ago or something like that. So it's been a long, long while.

 

Would you like to go back? Do you still have any family there?

I do have family there. We’ve never been super close, but I do have family there. I would always love to go back, but it's been really difficult because of the years and years of separation. Obviously, growing up in the Netherlands is hugely different, and then the UK is hugely different. A lot of my values, my culture, and my opinions have been shaped to be quite different to what's often the dominant culture in Morocco or what my family aligns with. I think that's the difficulty with my relationship with Morocco, because it's always going to be attached to my connection with my Moroccan family, which has been so-so. We're very different in the way that we think. We have very different beliefs, very different opinions. I think it's always going to be a weird relationship with the country because of that.

 

By the sounds of it, integrating into the UK has been a lot easier. I’m assuming the culture feels more natural to you?

The culture feels super natural, yeah. It was really difficult with language at first when I came to the country at ten or eleven, I remember struggling a lot to fit in. You know how kids can be. Not very nice when you don't fit in. But as the years have gone by, it's been so much easier to integrate. Even with the Netherlands, I remember visiting three years ago, and there were parts that felt like home – I was able to speak the language that I haven't spoken in a public setting in such a long time – but there are lots of things that have happened and moved on since I've been gone. So many cultural references that I just don't know. Actors I don't know, singers I don’t know.

I've spent so many years here being surrounded by that: watching British television, going to school in England, listening to the music on BBC Radio. Especially in my years as a teenager or a preteen. It's been much easier, especially speaking in 2026, to feel at home here.

 

Would you say you can feel at home in both places or instead that neither place is truly home?

I think none of them will be 100% home. I think England is like 80, 90% there. As I said, there's always going to be a distance because of the colour of my skin, my name, my accent, things like that. It's not going to make it super easy to always blend into the crowd. Once again, people say this out of curiosity, but they always end up – not from any fault of their own – separating me from the group. ‘Oh, there's that one girl, where is she from?’ and then it makes you remember, ‘oh yeah, I'm not from here’. So that's always going to be a challenge. But I would say England would be 80, 90% home. The Netherlands would be 60%, and Morocco is probably the biggest challenge I've had relating to culture and the country.

 

Would you like to have one place that is 100% home or are you comfortable with the idea that you're just from multiple places?

I think it's like a double edged sword in a certain sense. On one hand, I really admire people who have a home. The way I view home is kind of a fantasy concept because even in the Netherlands I was always a little bit of an outsider, especially since in my formative years I was in really small towns that weren't very diverse. So I've always felt as an outsider. My opinion about home is tainted by that; I never really felt it. When I see people who have their own culture they relate to, it feels almost like having your own family. Obviously you can appreciate everything else, but you've got your home base, the thing that feels like that sense of warmth, that thing that transcends wherever you are. I envy that sometimes. For example, when I'm talking to people and they're saying they're going back home to visit their family in said country, whichever they may be, or when I'm at a party and two people are from the same dominant culture and they just really hit it off, I sometimes envy that and admire that.

But I think there is also a good part of it. I think… Obviously my experience in Morocco has been limited, but at least with the Netherlands and England, I think it gave me a fresh perspective, and because I don't feel super stationed in any country, I feel like I've developed quite an open mindset. It made me much more open to the possibilities of different ways of life, different cultures, the ability to just move, and different ideas. Because that's often what cultures are: they're different ideas, different ways of living. I guess I've become more open as a result. That's the good side.

 

Do you see yourself making use of that then and moving around further?

I feel like the way I think about England has been quite practical. My mum, on the other hand, often talks about going back to the Netherlands, and for her she has that feeling of home. Each time I ask her about what it is that’s drawing her back to the Netherlands, it's always a feeling. It's not necessarily the healthcare, or whatever metric you want to use. It's ‘I want to go back home’. For me, it's always been more superficial, if that's the right word. I'm here because I've got friends here, but I'm here because it's really good for my career as well. It's one of the best places to study and practise law in the world. It's a great location, England, when it comes to being able to move into Europe. It's in the middle of almost everything. But if these factors change, as much as I'd love to stay here since I've built my life here, I'd be open to leaving. If I find out that Germany or wherever becomes the new legal powerhouse, it won't be long until I'll be out of here.

But one thing that is important to note is the UK and the Netherlands were both within the EU. So I feel like because I've spent my whole life within that context, my heart does come back to Europe. Even if it's not England or not the Netherlands, I think it'd be challenging – not impossible, but challenging – to leave the continent altogether. If there's a super-duper convincing reason for me to go to the Americas or Asia, I won't ever say no. But I think I have a little bias to this little continent.

 

Do you have some sense of European identity?

I think so. It's interesting, because I talked a lot in this conversation about the feeling of home. Although I didn't feel that with the Netherlands or England, I do feel that sometimes with Europe. Like, for example, my boyfriend is from Poland. When I visit Poland and I see the same ice cream brand I saw in the Netherlands, I feel a rush, or nostalgia. Or when I go to Germany and I see a similar cartoon character that was really popular when I was growing up in the Netherlands, it just brings joy to me, which is interesting. I feel like there are certain things that connect the continent. Certain songs that play on the radio that are super popular in Europe, where you're like ‘oh wow, we do have things in common.’ I think my feeling of European identity is coming from that.

 

Okay. And have you been around much of Europe then? You mentioned Germany and Poland.

Yeah, not a lot. I want to do more. I've briefly been to Belgium as a child. I've been to Spain when I was in secondary school. I was part of a youth choir and performed there. Germany, in the winter. Poland – I've been going almost every year now. That's been a huge hub. My boyfriend has much more of a tight-knit connection to his culture and his family. Much more than mine. So we always end up there, whether it be his hometown, Łódź, or anywhere else. I've been on trips to France. Growing up, my family didn't travel too much, to be honest. I'm always trying to catch up on it now because it's not something I did a lot as a child, which is funny, because we moved countries, but we didn't really go on many holidays across Europe or beyond. Yeah, just little trips here and there that I've tried to make time for.

 

So you've talked about being caught between Dutch and British cultures. What would you say are the similarities and differences between those?

It's really hard to say because I've been away from the Netherlands so much, so I'm always wary of being the Dutch culture expert. Sometimes people ask me about how things are in the Netherlands and I always have to preface by saying ‘I haven't been there in a while’. But if you're talking about my transition, I think culturally they're very similar. They're not far away, so that makes sense. A lot of the media you grow up watching is identical. In some respects, the Netherlands has much more of an honest, frank culture. People don't beat around the bush. If they have an opinion or they think you're doing something wrong or they don't like to do something, they will be a bit more honest about it than you’ll often see in England.

But funnily enough, even though this is true, I didn't have the hardest time with this because – maybe it’s because I spent more of my socialising years in the UK – I felt like I'm much more aligned to the British way of talking than the very honest, frank Dutch way. There are definitely small details like that, but it's not been super difficult for me to navigate. I'm sure if I moved here now, at twenty-three, from the Netherlands to England, I would notice that more. When I meet people from the Netherlands who moved here a bit older, or international students, I think they notice these cultural things way more than I did when I was ten years old.

 

Yeah, I definitely think that you seem more British than Dutch in the way that you speak compared to the blunt attitude that most Dutch people have.

Yeah it’s funny, I was at Brighton beach not that long ago with my friend from Canada, and we saw these firemen by the beach. I said to her, ‘why don't you go up to them and ask what's going on?’ just out of curiosity. And I thought to myself, ‘why don't I just ask?’. So I went up to the firemen, and they answered. My Canadian friend, she's like, ‘oh, I'm so proud of you, well done!’ and she turns to the fireman, ‘I was just saying to her, she's so British, you know? She's always too shy to speak up’. I notice that she often says, ‘she's so British, she's so British’. I don't know how I feel about that. I think it's true that I'm culturally British, but it felt weird to be called British because of how many times I've been asked where I'm from in this country. So culturally I am quite assimilated, I think.

 

You mentioned you found it much easier to integrate since you moved when you were a lot younger. But your father would have left Morocco for the Netherlands when he was about your age now, right? Not only that, but he left to cross a much broader cultural gap and then again left the Netherlands to come here. So how do you think your experience has compared to his?

Yeah, it's hard to say. I will preface this by saying he passed away six years ago, so I don't know how up to date my knowledge is. I didn't really notice how much of a big change that was for him until I started my uni journey. I used to think I’ll have such difficulty moving to a different city – from Bracknell to Brighton – and I couldn't imagine moving to a country with a completely different culture and language. The Netherlands and Morocco are culturally really different, even though it does help that there is a Moroccan community in the Netherlands.

I don't know too much about his personal experience moving to the Netherlands. I know that he struggled with the language, as did I when I moved to England. On the other hand, England is even more complicated because my father moved first when he was in his teens to start a degree in Glasgow, but it didn't work out. He had to leave to Morocco again for a good few years, and then he ended up in the Netherlands to properly do his degree in his twenties. He stayed there until he moved to England. So I guess to him it wasn't super different as he's been to Britain before and he spoke English at that point. I imagine that the move from Morocco to the Netherlands was definitely the harder one.

 

Speaking of the Moroccan community in the Netherlands, it certainly feels here like the topic of non-European migration has got very toxic within the last few years. From what I understand, the Dutch Moroccan community specifically are one of the main targets of this rhetoric. Do you know what your family thinks about that? 

Growing up in the Netherlands, I think you're quite aware if you come from a Moroccan lineage that you are the minority, and there are people that have opinions about that. Since then, after moving from my small town in the Netherlands to England, I've had distance from the discourse. So I'm not a Dutch expert, it's quite limited to my childhood memories and that specific town. I do hear that things are, as in many places in Europe, getting more tense about immigration and assimilation and all those things.

I'm a Dutch national, but I'm ethnically Moroccan, but I reside in the UK. For a lot of people, their nationality and their ethnicity are the same, but in my case it's not. My family are ethnically Moroccan, but on my mum’s side, all of them have Dutch citizenship, and not all of them have a Moroccan passport. It's really interesting to see their opinions about politics in the Netherlands, because you would assume that they would support politicians that are a little bit more left-leaning as opposed to those who are anti-immigration. But since they have the Dutch passport, they align themselves so much with their citizenship.

I remember my mum being like ‘I really hope we get a more right-leaning politician in the Netherlands. because I'm so tired of these immigrants taking advantage of us. I think Dutch citizens should be prioritised and I think that's the way it should be.’ I said ‘you're an immigrant…’, she's like, ‘no, I have a Dutch passport, and all of these asylum seekers are taking everything from us’. I remember thinking that this is so strange, all of them are ethnically Moroccan. But you can make a case that she was born there, she was raised there, she was completely assimilated. She's relatively white passing as well. It makes sense that she has that tie to her Dutch side, but it is really still interesting to see minority groups being quite against immigration, even though they wouldn't be able to be there without it, you know?

 

From what you’ve said, it almost sounds as if you're more connected to that Moroccan side than your mother is. Would you say that’s the case?

I think it goes back to the issue where as a third culture child, your depiction of your country – one that you have never lived in or weren't born in – is always going to be tainted by your opinion of your family. Those are the ones you always visit, those are the ones that give you the guide into what Moroccan culture is. That's usually all you get, unless you make lots of friends there. I think my mum has that issue, where it's mainly my father's side of the family residing in Morocco. She's had a difficult relationship with them, which is always going to taint Morocco for her, and I don't see any drive to want to visit the country at all.

But on the other hand, when she's in the UK, I always see her finding Moroccan, Middle Eastern, or Arab communities as opposed to Dutch communities. Obviously, you can say that there are fewer Dutch people, especially in Bracknell. But it seems she does feel a certain pride for Morocco, even though she wasn't born or raised there either. When she meets someone from Africa generally, or from Morocco or a neighbour like Egypt, her eyes light up, and she's so excited to make friends and connect with them over that.

So although there are aspects about Morocco that she thinks so fondly about, I think the idea of actually living there or visiting has become really difficult for her due to family. I think my mum's opinions – she identifies as Muslim as her parents did, and she's quite conservative in belief – means that often she has opinions that are quite similar to those who have immigrated from Morocco to the UK, for example.

I think I'm different, because the fact that I'm not really religious makes it even harder for me to connect with Moroccan culture, even if it's not in Morocco. I'm pretty left-leaning; I've always had those political beliefs, and even more as I grew up and went to university, which makes it a little bit harder. So on the whole, I would say we both have quite a difficult relationship with Morocco, but I think my mum somehow remains way more connected with it than I do.

 

Speaking of university, you mentioned before that you were a little intimidated just going from Bracknell to Brighton. How did you find that transition? Do you like Brighton?

That's so interesting; Bracknell has felt like home because it is home. I spent almost all of my years in England there. Brighton has only been four years, but it feels like home. It was really difficult moving here at first because it was different culturally, in the sense that it's a much bigger city. There's so much to do, it was intimidating. It was this huge student town with lots of young people, and I always struggled socialising with people growing up. My mum was quite conservative and she made it quite difficult to do stuff like sleepovers or go to parties – God forbid. [laughs] God forbid.

It was exciting, but scary, to go to a place where I'm deciding these things for myself. Going from having to push back on my mum a lot just to do normal things like going to a friend's house, to being able to decide what I'm doing, when, and where. I think the cultures also reflect that. Brighton is such an open city. People are so diverse in thought, and it is quite left-leaning, which aligns closer to my values. So it was a huge change, but Brighton really became home. I met lots of people that align with the way I see the world.

I remember I spent two months in South Korea a few years ago for a summer school. I had so much fun, it was a great time and really a highlight in my life so far, but when I got the train into Brighton station, I was like ‘finally, I'm home’. And I thought, why am I saying that? It was only after one or two years of being in Brighton. I felt like there was huge weight to being able to think that I fit in. Maybe that's also attributed to Brighton being super quirky, so it's pretty hard not to fit in. I think you can be quite a quirky, strange person and still somehow not be the weirdest person in the room. So I guess all of these things have nuance. Yeah, it's feeling much more like home.

 

Do you think you'll stay in Brighton?

Yeah, for the short term, I'm trying. In an ideal world where I didn't have to think of factors like my career and future development, I think the chances would be high. Obviously, I have to think about those things, so I will always go for the city or the country that's able to provide the most. I also think there is a lot of value in being able to leave a place, so even in a case where Brighton was amazing for my career, I would want to leave at least for a couple of years. Not just the city, maybe even the country. Life is short, and it's really important that you get to experience different ways of life and as much of what life is, which isn't just Brighton.

 

Where would you go for a few years?

That's tricky. I always have conversations about this to friends, or to my boyfriend. It's really difficult to say. I've been very dictated by my career, and I'm really interested in tech law, so places like Germany are quite attractive for me, and Germany gets that bonus of being a little bit close to home. It's not super different from the Netherlands or England, it's kind of a blend in that sense. But if I didn't have to think about that, it’d be much trickier. I'd be open to anywhere if it's only a few years. I'm happy to just see where life takes me. That's how I got to England, right? My father made a career choice, I didn't, and it ended up okay. I'm happy to see where things take me. But as I said earlier, there's this home feeling of Europe. So if you're talking about settling down, I don't think I would leave Europe.

 

So you don't know where in Europe you would settle down, but you do think it would be Europe.

Yeah, maybe settling somewhere like Germany, because it feels so familiar. If I end up in England, I wouldn’t mind. If I end up in the Netherlands, I wouldn’t mind. I think it's important, especially when you're younger, to be open, because you never know what the perfect place is for you or whether it's somewhere you never thought to look.

 

Okay. Last question then. Can you think of one artist from your culture – and I'm leaving that deliberately vague – that you particularly like, and that represents some of your culture as well?

I find that really interesting. I'm not super knowledgeable in the arts, which I would love to be more. I find people who are really aware and engage with that a lot really cool, even if it's film or music. But I've never been like that. I think, unfortunately, a lot of my years in the Netherlands and England were super influenced by the dominant American culture, which made it hard for me to connect with Dutch or English artists. If I think about my childhood, I think a lot about American TV shows on Nickelodeon, or American pop hits on the radio.

Ironically, even though I don't feel part of my Moroccan culture anymore, part of me is thinking back to when I was a young child, like five, six, seven years old. I remember my family always putting Nancy Ajram on. She’s really popular in Morocco. She's a Lebanese singer, actually. It's funny, because she’s not even Moroccan, and I'm not even that attached to Moroccan culture, but it represents such an innocent memory of Moroccan culture. Away from my fears about not fitting in, or my lack of religious beliefs, or my opinions about my family. Hearing that on the radio, going back to Morocco, or even just in the living room in my house in the Netherlands… Even if I didn't always know what the lyrics meant, the joy of the sound of the songs, and the dancing of my family in the kitchen is a core memory of mine. It goes back to how it's not always about rationalising a culture, but the feeling aspect as well.

In your own words, where are you from, where did you grow up, where are your family from? What's your background?

Well, I'm from Barcelona, and other than Barcelona, I would say I'm from Catalonia. Those are the terms that mostly describe where I come from. And yeah, my family, all of them are from Catalonia, my parents and my grandparents.

My parents come from Reus, it's like one and a half hours south from Barcelona. My parents met in Barcelona during their studies, and then my sister and I were born there, and we grew up in Barcelona, in the city. But we still have a lot of connection with Reus – it's a smaller city – because our family is still there. So I also consider myself from Reus as well, because my family actually comes from there. But yeah, mostly Barcelona.

 

Okay, do you see any cultural differences between these two cities?

I would say for sure, in the sense that Barcelona is such a big city, so there is no such culture as ‘Barcelona’, because nowadays there are more tourists or people that come from other places than actual Barcelonians that have been living there forever. So Reus feels more Catalan, or like… not Catalan necessarily, but it’s more on a smaller scale, and everyone knows each other a little bit, even though it's still over 100,000 people. But it feels different for sure, more traditional. There are still some traditions conserved there, more than in Barcelona, which is a cosmopolitan, metropolitan city.

 

And you're saying Catalan then – am I to assume that you feel more Catalan than Spanish?

Yes, indeed. Yeah, I feel like ‘Catalan’ represents me.

 

Okay, and Spanish is not even a second identity for you or…?

I would never say out of my mouth, ‘I am Spanish’ or ‘I feel Spanish’, but there are people that don't know the reality or the difference between Catalonia and Spain, and they would say, ‘oh, you come from Spain’, and then I wouldn’t say every time ‘no, no, no, no, I am from Catalonia’. But when I have the chance to present myself, I would always present myself as Catalan, or as Barcelonian, and not as Spanish.

 

So what would you say are the differences between Catalan and Spanish identity?

There are lots of differences. Historically, of course, when there were the two kingdoms of Castile and Aragon. These were two different kingdoms with different traditions, even different languages. And then they united, but the culture and the history has always grown separately, like it was never really unified. Even though the territory unified, the people didn’t. So I would say there’s a historical component for sure, and also a cultural one.

You just have to go there, like Catalan people in the way that they talk, and in the way that there are a lot of stereotypes that are specifically targeted to Catalan people and not to Spanish people. We have different festivities; we have different traditions for Christmas that only Catalans do. So there are different components that I would say differentiate us.

 

Is your connection to Catalan culture something that's primarily about the traditions, the language, or the place itself? What is it that makes Catalan identity an identity?

For me, definitely knowing the whole history and traditions, which is very linked to language. I would say language is one of the core characteristics. Catalan developed parallel to Spanish; we're all Latin languages, but there is still a difference, and from the language we have our own linguistic movements and our own ways of expressing ourselves. So I think that is a very important feature of Catalan identity.

 

And is the language similar to other Romance languages or is it quite different?

No, it's actually pretty similar. I would say it's a mix between Spanish and French. And in some cases, like grammar and how the words are written, it's closer to French than to Spanish, but the pronunciation is obviously very different to French. The pronunciation is closer to Spanish, but the way you write and the grammar is closer to French. So it's a mix.

 

Is there a standard Catalan dialect or is it very diverse?

Actually, Catalan Countries – you’d normally talk about Andorra, Catalonia, the Community of València, and the Balearic Islands – they all have their different dialects of Catalan. For example in València, they speak Valencian. It's Catalan, I understand them, but they have a dialect. In the islands it's the same, and even inside of Catalonia, the ones from the south or the ones from the north have small accents, but you would always understand each other. It's not that different that you would not understand it, they’re small dialects, but there is a difference.

 

Growing up there, is it easy to use Catalan as a first language, or is Spanish sometimes more predominant?

That's a huge problem actually. I remember in the past I could use it more broadly, but since 2011, let's say, when all the demonstrations started about independence, Catalan has been very much linked to politics. So very broadly, if you speak Catalan you're seen as independentist, and that harmed the Catalan language a lot, because a lot of people didn't want to speak Catalan because of politics. Before that it was actually very normal to speak Catalan in society, but nowadays when I go back to Barcelona? Forget it – I cannot speak only Catalan during the whole day, it's impossible, not even once.

In Reus or in other places, in towns, for sure I would say Catalan is still very very present. You can go through daily life only speaking Catalan, but in Barcelona that is not possible anymore. And that's very sad, because it has been politicised, and it's now actually in danger of starting on the way to extinction. I know it won't happen, and I really hope not, but it's in danger, it's a fact.

 

So in Barcelona is it the case that people still understand it but they don't speak it for political reasons, or…?

Actually it's both. There is this part obviously, but I would say that’s everywhere in Catalonia generally. In Barcelona specifically, the problem is immigration. Not a problem in the sense that I don't want it, but that it's really like that. Mostly from Latin America, since they speak Spanish – and in Catalonia you can also speak Spanish, because it's bilingual; normally everyone that speaks Catalan also speaks Spanish, except maybe older people in the small villages – and since they speak Spanish, they don't make the effort sometimes to learn Catalan, because it's also not required in a lot of jobs. In public institutions it is, but other than that, normally it’s not.

In Barcelona now also, the big, big problem we have is that a lot of people come as digital nomads, and they come for one or two years and they leave, and they obviously won't learn Catalan. And actually more than immigration, the problem is this temporary migration, these nomads that just come because it's a nice city and a technological hub, and then leave.

 

You mentioned that everybody who speaks Catalan also speaks Spanish. Is everyone perfectly fluent in both, or is Spanish more of a second language for some?

I would say in cities, not only Barcelona but around Catalonia, Spanish and Catalan are at perfectly the same level. For smaller towns where they basically only socialise in Catalan, then maybe I would say it's not the same, Spanish is more like a second language. But mostly they speak both the same, and actually the opposite is more problematic. There are a lot of people that speak Spanish and know Catalan, but since they don't practice it, actually Catalan is the second language, even though they're Catalans and were born there and raised there and everything. They go to public schools in Catalan, they learn Catalan, they know Catalan, but they don't speak it, or they consider it as a second language.

 

So in schools, media, things like that, is Catalan the predominant language?

In public schools it should be, but the fact is that it's not. There was also a huge debate about public schools actually. Last year or a couple of years ago the Spanish government wanted to impose that public schools should be taught in at least 25% Spanish, because they were considering that Spanish was in danger in Catalonia since they only speak Catalan. But actually, if you go to public schools – and I know because my dad works in one, and I have family and friends there – the reality is that even though classes in public schools should be taught in Catalan, if the majority of people speak Spanish, the teacher adapts to the pupils. So actually, I would be happy if only 25% of subjects would be taught in Spanish, but the reality is quite the opposite, most of them are taught in Spanish even though they should be in Catalan in public schools.

 

Where else have you lived outside of Barcelona?

I've lived in Germany for my bachelor's and now for my master's. I lived in Brussels for some months for Erasmus, I also lived in Mexico for almost a year, and now in Strasbourg, also for some months. As for living, I would say that's it.

 

Do you think that those experiences have had a big influence on you?

Of course, all of them. Yeah, yeah, yeah, definitely.

 

How so?

Very differently. I mean, it's not the same when you're eighteen and going to a different country as when you're twenty-three and going to Mexico. Germany was very much an experience that helped me mature a lot, because I was on my own at eighteen going to study. I didn’t have my parents nearby where I could go on the weekends, so there I learnt a lot as a person, and I also love my studies. Also, adapting to a different society. It helped me a lot to know myself, how I am and what I like.

For the other places, I would say everything was also growth, but from a more mature place, and more just from gaining experience. They all were very valuable experiences for myself personally, and also to know where I want to work in, what my passions are, and what I really want to do in this life.

 

And what is it that you're studying in Germany?

I'm doing my master's degree in International Relations: Peace and Conflict Studies in Frankfurt.

 

And what is it that attracts you to that subject?

Well, actually because I really like politics, and because where I come from in Catalonia, you're confronted with politics. It's always this tension between Spain and Catalonia and all the politics. So I was always interested in politics, and then I started also being interested in international politics, and seeing this feeling of injustice. I was feeling it while I was at school, like ‘why are things unjust?’, thinking about migration and wars. I thought ‘I want to do something to make a better world’, but I really do want to inform myself more about what conflicts are going on around the world, and which instruments there are now to influence them.

 

Do you speak German then?

Yes, I learnt it at school.

 

Do you speak any other languages?

I speak English, Catalan and Spanish obviously, German, and then I would say the one I speak worst is French. I learnt them all at school. When I was in Barcelona, I learnt them all at school, and then at university I continued with French.

 

Having lived both in French and German speaking countries, do you think that speaking those languages is an essential part of understanding those cultures, or is it more just a way of communication?

Communication is very important, to avoid misunderstandings it’s better if you share the same language, but I think culturally, if you're able to speak the language, you have more opportunities to engage in local activities. When I was in Germany, I knew many friends that came from Barcelona or elsewhere who could only communicate in English and not German, and they were very limited, most of them only had friends from their own countries. I also think Nordic cultures are a bit more closed, so it's even more important to speak the same language. The language tells much more about what expressions they have, how the humour is, how they express themselves. It tells a lot about how a society behaves, so I think that's important. 

Catalan is also a very good example, because I think knowing the language tells a lot about the people. Which expressions they use, which references they make, that tells a lot about our socialisation and our history, so I think that's what makes it important for the culture.

 

With Catalan then, what does the language tell you about the culture?

I think Catalan language historically – just the existence of the language – has been a sign that we're a society that doesn’t give up. It's a culture that doesn't give up. During the dictatorship of Franco in Spain, Catalan was prohibited, so at school, or in the streets even, you could not speak Catalan. So for the people that speak Catalan in their families, in their houses, it was a sign of resistance, a sign that we're not giving up. Through history there are a lot of examples, and for me even the mere fact of speaking Catalan is a sign that I'm not giving up on this language, and I'm resisting. But it also tells about Catalan culture, like when I speak Catalan to my parents, just the tone of voice, how you speak, and the expressions you use, I would say that is a very Catalan thing. We have a lot of phrases for everything, we use a lot of expressions. It's very expressive, and that also characterises Catalan people.

 

Would you say Catalan people are quite open?

I consider myself open, but I wouldn't say actually that Catalan people are directly super open like you can imagine when you think about south Spain. Like Andalusian people, they would even speak to stones, you know? Like they would speak to a plant, they don't care. Catalans aren’t that sense of open, but I would say it's a very welcoming society. So I do think you get along, but maybe it takes some time.

 

And you said you were in Mexico for almost a year right? What were you doing there?

I was volunteering through a Catalan organisation that cooperates with three cities in Mexico that are all border cities. It's very much about the reality of the border, and the challenges and complications that come with the border. They cooperate with this religious entity – they're called Escolapios – and then we went there to mostly work on local projects with youth.

 

Would you say that religion is also an important part of culture to you?

To me personally, yes. I wouldn't say our society. In Mexico religion is very present, everywhere where you go. I would say even in Latin America generally. In Catalonia or in Spain, I wouldn't say it is at all, at least for our generation, but I would say for me it's important.

 

Why do you think it's not so important for most people in Catalonia?

Well, it's pretty obvious that there have been a lot of scandals. It's more linked to institutions, so if you link religion to institutions and not to faith, then obviously distrust comes, because humankind is corrupt and there are bad people everywhere. The institution is corrupting faith, so I think as a result of the scandals, it’s to go against that.

 

You've lived all over Europe – can you imagine yourself ever leaving Catalonia forever, or would you be drawn to go back eventually?

I’ve thought about it a lot, and I know that those are my roots, and I feel very proud of being where I come from, and I want the best thing for Catalonia. It's difficult, but at the same time, I think if I were to go back now it would limit me too. Because the reality is that there are not so many jobs, there are not so many prospects, at least in the sector where I am now. So I think yes, I would like to go back, but at the same time I've also been building my network and my friendships in Germany now, for example, so I also consider Germany as a place to live. I think someday I will go back, but for now I do think that for what I'm searching for in my life, other places can give me other opportunities.

 

Do you feel connected to Germany then?

Yeah, yeah I do actually.

 

Do you feel German?

No, not ever. I could never feel German even if I had the ID. As we have been talking about, it comes with an identity, it comes with a culture, it comes with a sentiment, and my sentiment will always be Catalan.

 

But I think the longer you spend somewhere, integrated into that society, the more that culture affects you.

For sure, I've noticed also from the first year I was in Germany to now, I do some things now that I would never have done in the first year. So I'm adapting to the German culture, but still for me Catalonia, and my family there, is an essential part of my being. I'm very familiar with it, so I always love to go back home and want to go back home. Of course, I could adapt and I could very much feel at home in Germany, but I would never feel German.

 

Do you have any examples of things that you've caught yourself doing in Germany that you wouldn't have done before?

Well, one silly thing about the weather – in Barcelona it never rains, so for me when it rains, I stay home. In Germany, at least where I was in Düsseldorf, it rained the whole time, and for the first month I was just not leaving home in the afternoons, because I was giving the excuse ‘no, it's raining, so I'm not coming’. At some point I realised ‘Glòria, you have to start doing things when it rains as well, because it's the reality here’, so then I started to accept the rain.

 

Do you have any favourite Catalan traditions?

I have a couple, but I would say one of my favourites is on Christmas. It's basically a chunk of wood with a face drawn on – ‘caga tió’, it’s the chunk of wood and also the tradition – that you bring home one month before Christmas. You traditionally go, then, to search for them in the woods, and then you bring them home and give them food so that they eat a lot before Christmas. Then on Christmas Day, you cover them with blankets, go to the kitchen, and sing Christmas songs. Then you go back and hit them with a stick while singing a very specific song, and afterwards you open the blankets and see that beneath the blankets there are lots of gifts. So the logic is that the ‘caga tió’ has eaten so much that at Christmas he shits the presents, basically. It's amazing, I love it, we do it on Christmas and it's only in Catalonia, nowhere else in the world.

 

 

That's fantastic.

it is, it's very fun.

 

And that's in all Catalan regions or…?

I don't know actually, I don't know if they do it in the Balearic Islands, or in València. I know in Catalonia for sure.

 

What's the distinction then between Catalonia and the Catalan regions?

Catalonia is where Barcelona is, and Barcelona is like the capital of the Catalan Countries, and that's why Catalan culture has been pretty centralised in Catalonia only. Now they're trying more to also give a voice to Catalan singers from the islands, or from València, but normally the Catalan culture was coming from Catalonia, so that's why. It's also where it has been more preserved. For example, if you go to the south of València that's closer to Andalusia, there are places where they don't speak Catalan anymore, so that's why Catalonia is considered like the ‘capital’.

 

How do you feel about Catalan independence?

That's very political, this could be one hour more. I feel like every community has the right broadly to decide what they want to be, and I do think that Catalonia historically and culturally has grown separately from Spain, as I said, more than unified as part of Spain. So personally I am for independence, but beyond that, I am for the right of people to self-determination generally.

 

And when you're thinking about independence – not practically but theoretically – is this for Catalonia or for the Catalan Countries?

Andorra is already a country. So there’s not so much to do there [laughs]. They managed. I think again, right of self-determination, everything should go through the people. People should decide, everything should go through a referendum I believe. I haven’t thought about that, so I don't have a strong opinion on how it should look, but if people want it, then it should be, and if people don't want it, then it shouldn't.

 

So you don't necessarily feel so strongly attached to the other Catalan Countries, or…?

I feel kind of like brothers and sisters. Like we’re all the same, but I also recognise that historically and geographically there are differences. So I also acknowledge the right to self-determination, so that they can also decide what they want to be. But I do feel attached to Catalan Countries.

 

Okay. Just because you're talking about each community having its own right to decide, but then that kind of implies that those are different communities.

Yeah, that's true. But legally, they are different communities. We have autonomous communities, so Catalonia could only decide for Catalonia. If we wanted the Balearic Islands to be also on a referendum, the Balearic Islands would have to request a referendum to Spain themselves. So we're not unified now, it has to work separately. For now, because I was brought up and grew up in Catalonia, since Catalonia is the one concerned, then I'm fighting for Catalonia. If the Balearic Islands also want independence, I will fight with them too, but I cannot fight for them.

 

Would you say you’re close with Spanish people in the same way that you feel close to the other Catalan peoples?

I feel attached to people generally, and Spanish bonds us too because I speak Spanish, so  there is a bonding inevitably. I have Spanish friends of course, it's not like I have hatred or something against Spanish people, no. So it binds me in the sense of the language.

 

But it's just because you speak the language and because you live there, it’s not that you feel close?

Exactly.

 

Okay. How would you compare the Catalan situation to the Basque situation?

Well I would say it's pretty different. Again historically, again with the relations they have with Spain, and the history with terrorism, and X and Y. It's very different from the relations that Catalonia has with Spain, and the history of Catalonia, so you can compare it in the sense of wanting independence, but it's a very different political struggle I would say.

 

Is there a sense of solidarity between those two communities?

That's the weird thing. I would think so, that it would be logical, but actually there is not so much. My intuition would say because the Basque Country gets much more out from Spain than Catalonia does. I think if the Basque Country really wants something it's more probable that the Spanish government will hear them, but the Catalan people not so much. I think also because Catalonia is more economically important to Spain, so they have more sentiment of keeping Catalonia than Basque. It's just a different relationship.

 

Okay. And the cultures are quite different?

Yeah, yeah, of course. I don't know Basque culture so much but I know it's very, very different.

 

Okay. Coming from the UK, I'd say there are parallels drawn in the UK between the case of Catalonia to Spain and Scotland to the UK. Is there anything from your side? Do you ever see that compared?

Yeah, you always see in the Catalan demonstrations on the 11th of September – that's our national day – there are always Scottish representatives with Scottish flags. Not so many, but some. And I don't know so much about Scottish history to be able to draw an analytical comparison, but I think there is a kind of comparison.

But for us it's always seeing Scotland as the big brother, in the sense of ‘this is how it should look’, and in our case ‘this is the reality’. Great Britain for us was a democratic country that gave at least one opportunity to the people to vote on their future, and with Spain we are not dealing with a democratic country as we compare it. They don't give us the choice to vote. So we always see Scotland as a success story, or at least that they're dealing with a democratic country.

 

So the situation in Scotland is seen more favourably then?

Well better in terms of… at least they could have a referendum. So looking up and working towards that, while knowing the realities are very different, the central governments are very different – like London from Madrid – the societies, and everything. But there is this belief.

 

Okay. Do you think there's some solidarity there then?

Yeah, yeah. Of course. There’s not solidarity in the sense that we really work together, but there is this collective solidarity where you would say ‘I understand you, I don't know so much about you, but I understand you at least’.

 

Are there any other cases that you would compare it to?

Well, there's always the Quebec one, but I think that is also very different. Other than that, I would say those are the most common.

 

Is there anything more you want to add before the last question? 

I would just add that I've come across a lot of people who want to put this tension, like ‘you're independentist or not’ and link being Catalan with politics, or trying to create that tension between Spanish and Catalan, and for me it's not like a football team, you know? For me, you really have to understand the history and the culture everywhere. Not just in this case. But I think that's very important to understand, because there's never just black and white. There are always nuances and there are always good things and bad things in every decision.

So if Catalonia would ever be independent, of course that would come with risks. It's not an ideal society. We would also have a populist extremist right, because we're not an ideal society, it's pretty obvious. But it always comes with risks, so you should not prejudge without knowing. You should always get to know the culture and the people, and talk with whoever is actually affected by those decisions, or what you're going through. So I would say that is very important, to not just get the headlines, but to try to inform yourself a little bit more.

 

Last question then, could you pick out one artist from your culture – it could be a musician, author, writer, painter, anything – who really speaks to you, and connects with you on the level of representing your culture?

I would say a singer called Lluís Llach. He's probably seventy-something now. There are a lot of singers and Catalan artists that I really love, but he was the first one that came to mind, because during the dictatorship, during Franco, he was doing songs that were implicitly criticising it, but doing so in a very intelligent way. He was always fighting for the Catalan struggle from his artistic way, and was always fighting – and is still – fighting for a plural, inclusive Catalan society. And always with this sentiment that I've also tried to show, that we have a very unique identity – as everyone else does – but it's very precious, and to try to explain where it comes from, the roots, and the feeling. So I think he's a very good singer, he has very good songs, and he represents Catalan culture and Catalan identity very well.

entry.content:
Can you tell me a bit in your own words about where you're from and where you grew up?

I was born in Belgrade, I grew up in the suburbs of Belgrade. I'm deeply attached, in terms of identity, to the city, to its history and culture, much like my parents. I would describe myself as very much rooted in Belgrade, my family having changed locations numerous times, within the city and also outside in some cases, but we've always had a particular attachment to this city above all else, geographically speaking.

 

What do you think of Belgrade then? Do you like it as a city and a place to grow up?

Belgrade has gone through massive changes over the years, over the course of my life alone, let alone during the lives of my ancestors. It used to be the very center, the core of Yugoslavia, a large, multinational state which, for its time, had an outsized influence on the world stage. Now, though still a big city, it's the capital of a much smaller country, and I think one can easily feel it. 

I think the outside context, the context of the whole organism that is the country, influences Belgrade also, and the city has therefore gone through many changes, some of them good, some of them quite bad, a consequence of political decisions. I think what I like about Belgrade, and about growing up in Belgrade, is what I like about any other major European city, which is the sense of history, and a cosmopolitanism which you simply can't find in a smaller town. The city was built by various nationalities, not just Serbs.

 

Are you drawn to any other major European cities then, if they'd have the same historical and cosmopolitan appeal? Or are you content to stay in Belgrade in the future?

Well, when it comes to Belgrade, what makes it stand out is that it was the inflection point of numerous great civilizations. Cities like Prague and Paris, both of which I admire, grew up mostly within a singular context. Everywhere in Prague, you can feel the Austrian, Central European influence, in the architecture, in the way the streets are shaped, in the public squares and the spirit of the city, and so on. 

Belgrade, however, is a hodgepodge of different influences, and it has such a complicated history. You can feel the city's various occupations and its wounds just walking down almost any street. The city spent centuries under the Turks, and you can see the Ottoman influence in the city's central parts, the eastern bank of the Sava. Then, it was free, and it returned to European influences. On the western side, in Zemun, you feel like you're in any other Austro-Hungarian town, the exact kind of street layout common in their towns, with a main street and buildings with Baroque motifs. And then you have the historical influences - New Belgrade, built under communism, in Brutalist architecture. And then you have scars across the city due to the city's six times being bombarded, most recently in 1999.

Very few cities in Europe, I think, boast such a fascinating history. It has its own appeal, like any other city does. I am temperamentally closest to Western influences, so Paris, Prague, Vienna and the like feel spiritually closest to me, and I would feel at home there the most, as I do with such elements here already.

 

So, where do you think Belgrade - and Serbia - sits in respect to these different civilisations now? It feels to me as if Serbia is still at the crossroads of East and West, now between Russia and Europe. Where do you think Serbia's place is culturally and politically?

I think it's fair to describe Belgrade and Serbia as quite the basketcase on the European and world stage. I think, at first glance, it feels like any other place in Europe, but then you dig deeper, and you look at the Serbian mindset, and I think you find that we have always resisted easy definition. 

Serbia is nowadays portrayed, in some media, as a Russian offspring, but as a matter of fact, while there has always been a cultural and religious affinity, we spent most of the 20th century estranged from Russia, and culturally-speaking there was very much an affinity for America, for Coca-Cola, for blue jeans and rock music and so on. We have always I think been both that kind of ordinary European, Western-looking Serbia, and a Serbia that very much has its own, how should I put it, parochial, inward-looking ways. I think that tension exists elsewhere, but with Serbia it's especially palpable, because, to this day, our national identity actually isn't all that clear. We spent half the 20th century as socialist Yugoslavs advocating non-alignment, and now we're post-socialist Serbs gravitating at once both westwards and eastwards and nowhere in particular. I view Serbia as a culturally European country, and perhaps that influences my direction politically, though I'm not very concerned with it on a personal level. I believe political alignments of any kind are really ephemeral, that there isn't really an end to history.

 

Do you personally feel any connection to a sense of wider European identity?

In terms of identity, I have always felt myself to be myself first and foremost. On a personal level, what I dislike most is when people subordinate their individual identities to some social identity, whether it's for a national identity, or a generational identity, or an ideological one. I believe the end result, ultimately, is the suspension of thought, the disappearance of the individual. But I have always felt myself connected to Europe, on a deep level, just as I feel connected to Serbia, within Europe, on a deep level. I believe both connections go much deeper than merely blood and soil, because I am what I am and wouldn't have been the same had I just been born elsewhere, you know, a hundred kilometers to the west or to the east, or even elsewhere within my own country, or my own city. To have brought up individuality might seem like a digression of mine, but really, I feel any person's identity is grounded at once in himself and in all the layers that lead up to humanity as a whole, from the family, to the city, to country, to broader civilizational context, and yes, I see myself connected to the European one and the European line in history.

 

In that case, could you tell me more about your individual circumstances? Are you working or studying, for instance?

Well, I'm doing both. Right now my studies are kind of on hold for various reasons, personal and non-personal, so I'm working at a major bookstore in the city center. I encounter lots of people, from all over the world, during the average workday. Working at a major bookstore, in a major national capital, is really good for cultivating a more global mindset, with the way it brings you into contact with so many people through mere circumstance.

 

And what is it that you're studying?

English language, literature and culture.

 

Why did you choose that subject?

I've had a lifelong fascination with American and British culture, as I saw them, the aspects that I saw.
